q: Which of the following is a synthetic adhesive?
x: Urea–methanal resin is made industrially from urea and methanal and is used, for example, to bond plywood. Starch paste, casein glue and animal glue come from natural materials.

q: Which property is typical of a thermoplastic adhesive?
o: It sets by forming a permanent cross-linked network
It needs a hardener mixed in just before use
It sets only when it absorbs moisture
It softens each time it is heated and hardens again on cooling
x: Thermoplastic adhesives have chains that are not cross-linked, so they melt and reset repeatedly. A permanent cross-linked network and a hardener are features of thermosetting adhesives.

q: A rubber-based contact adhesive is spread on both surfaces and left for a few minutes before they are pressed together. The waiting time allows:
o: The solvent to evaporate so the films become tacky
The resin and hardener to react
Moisture from the air to start polymerisation
The molten adhesive to cool and solidify
x: Contact adhesives are dissolved in a volatile solvent; once most of it evaporates, the tacky films bond instantly on contact. Resin and hardener describe epoxy adhesives.

q: Gum arabic, a natural adhesive used on envelopes and postage stamps, is obtained from:
x: Gum arabic is a plant gum collected from acacia trees and becomes sticky when moistened. Animal bones give animal glue and milk protein gives casein glue.

q: The force of attraction between an adhesive and the surface it is applied to is called:
x: Adhesion is attraction between different substances, here the glue and the surface. Cohesion is the attraction within the adhesive itself.

q: Silicone sealant adhesives are widely used around bathroom fittings and in aquariums because, once set, they:
x: Set silicone remains rubbery and is not attacked by water, so it seals wet joints that move slightly. A brittle or water-soluble adhesive would fail in these uses.

q: Compared with joining parts by rivets or bolts, an advantage of using an adhesive is that it:
o: Spreads the load over the whole bonded area and can join unlike materials
Always gives a joint stronger than the materials themselves
Can always be taken apart easily without damage
Works at any temperature without softening
x: An adhesive needs no holes, spreads stress evenly and can bond different materials such as metal to plastic. Adhesive joints are not always stronger than the materials and many soften when hot.

q: A dye differs from a pigment in that a dye:
o: Is insoluble and only coats the surface with a binder
Has no chromophore in its molecule
Is usually soluble in the dyeing medium and becomes attached to the fibre
x: Dyes are applied from solution and are taken up by or bound to the fibre. Pigments are insoluble particles held on the surface by a binder, as in paints.

q: Polyester fibres repel water and are difficult to dye. They are usually dyed with:
x: Disperse dyes are almost insoluble in water and are applied as a fine dispersion that dissolves into the hydrophobic polyester. Direct dyes are for cotton and acid dyes for wool, silk and nylon.

q: Basic (cationic) dyes, whose coloured part carries a positive charge, are mainly used to dye:
x: Acrylic fibres carry negative groups that attract the positive dye ions. On cotton, basic dyes need a mordant such as tannin, and polyester takes disperse dyes.

q: Alizarin, a red mordant dye, was originally obtained from:
o: The leaves of the indigo plant
The roots of the madder plant
x: Alizarin was extracted from madder roots before it was made synthetically. Indigo leaves give the blue dye indigo, and cochineal insects give a crimson dye.

q: The first synthetic dye, mauveine, was discovered by:
x: W. H. Perkin made mauveine by accident while trying to make quinine, which started the synthetic dye industry. Wöhler is known for making urea.

q: Azo dyes are prepared by coupling a diazonium salt with:
o: A phenol or an aromatic amine
x: An aryl diazonium ion reacts with an activated aromatic ring such as a phenol or an aromatic amine, joining the two rings through –N=N–. Alkanes and alkyl halides do not couple this way.

q: In a dye molecule, the main role of an auxochrome group such as –OH or –NH₂ is to:
o: Deepen the colour and help the dye attach to the fibre
Supply the colour on its own without a chromophore
Make the dye insoluble in water
Reduce the dye to a colourless form
x: The chromophore is responsible for colour; the auxochrome intensifies it and gives the dye a group that can bind to the fibre. Without a chromophore there is no colour.

q: Polystyrene is an addition polymer of:
x: Styrene (phenylethene) polymerises through its C=C bond to give polystyrene. Chloroethene gives PVC, propene gives polypropene and tetrafluoroethene gives Teflon.

q: When nylon-6,6 is made from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid, each amide link formed releases one molecule of:
x: –NH₂ of the diamine and –COOH of the acid join as –CO–NH– and lose H₂O, which is why this is condensation polymerisation. HCl is released only when the acid chloride is used instead.

q: Which polymer is a homopolymer, made from a single kind of monomer?
x: PVC is made only from chloroethene. Nylon-6,6 (diamine and diacid), Terylene (diol and diacid) and Bakelite (phenol and methanal) each need two different monomers.

q: Polythene softens when heated, but Bakelite does not. This is because Bakelite:
o: Is made of very short chains
x: Bakelite is a thermosetting polymer whose chains are joined by cross-links, so heating cannot make them slide past each other. Polythene has separate chains and is thermoplastic. Bakelite is a condensation polymer.

q: Low-density polythene (LDPE) is less dense than high-density polythene (HDPE) because its chains:
o: Are cross-linked into a rigid network
Are highly branched and cannot pack closely
Are only about ten units long
x: Branches keep LDPE chains apart, leaving more empty space, so the density is lower. HDPE has mostly straight chains that pack closely. Both are made of carbon and hydrogen only.

q: Polystyrene has the repeating unit –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–, of formula C₈H₈. A chain of 500 such units has a relative molecular mass of (C 12, H 1):
x: C₈H₈ = 8 × 12 + 8 × 1 = 104, and 104 × 500 = 52 000. 48 000 counts only the carbon atoms, and 5200 drops a zero.

q: The linkage that joins the repeating units in a polyester such as Terylene is:
x: A polyester forms when –COOH and –OH groups condense, giving ester links. The amide link –CO–NH– belongs to nylons.

q: The synthetic fibre Orlon (acrylic) is obtained by polymerising which monomer?
x: Acrylic fibres are addition polymers of acrylonitrile, CH₂=CHCN. Chloroethene gives PVC, and ethane-1,2-diol is a monomer of polyesters.
